<title>Ivy League</title>
<fragment>

Undergraduate enrollments range from about 4,500 to about 15,000,[13] larger than most liberal arts colleges and smaller than most state universities. Total enrollment, which includes graduate students, ranges from approximately 6,600 at Dartmouth to over 20,000 at Columbia, Cornell, Harvard, and Penn. Ivy League financial endowments range from Brown's $6.9 billion[14] to Harvard's $53.2 billion,[15] the largest financial endowment of any academic institution in the world.[16]


The Ivy League is similar to other groups of universities in other countries, such as the *Grandes écoles* in France,[17] Scotland's Ancient Universities, the Golden Triangle or Loxbridge[18] in England, the C9 League[19] in China, the Imperial Universities[20] in Japan, and the Group of Eight[21] in Australia.



## Members

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Ivy League universities have some of the largest university financial endowments in the world, allowing the universities to provide abundant resources for their academic programs, financial aid, and research endeavors. As of 2021, Harvard University had an endowment of $53.2 billion, the largest of any educational institution.[15] Each university attracts millions of dollars in annual research funding from both the federal government and private sources.

### Endowment

[edit]

Main article: Harvard University endowment

Harvard has the largest university endowment in the world, valued at about $50.7 billion as of 2023.[3][4]
During the recession of 2007–2009, it suffered significant losses that forced large budget cuts, in particular temporarily halting construction on the Allston Science Complex.[61]
The endowment has since recovered.[62][63][64][65]


About $2 billion of investment income is annually distributed to fund operations.[66]
Harvard's ability to fund its degree and financial aid programs depends on the performance of its endowment; a poor performance in fiscal year 2016 forced a 4.4% cut in the number of graduate students funded by the Faculty of Arts and Sciences.[67]
Endowment income is critical, as only 22% of revenue is from students' tuition, fees, room, and board.[68]

Yale University was founded as "the Collegiate School" in 1701. As of April 2021, 58 Nobel laureates, 29 Turing Award laureates,[note 1] and 8 Fields Medalists have been affiliated with Stanford as students, alumni, faculty, or staff.[40] In addition, Stanford is particularly noted for its entrepreneurship and is one of the most successful universities in attracting funding for start-ups.[41][42][43][44][45] Stanford alumni have founded numerous companies, which combined produce more than $2.7 trillion in annual revenue.[46][47][48] Stanford is the alma mater of U.S. President Herbert Hoover, the current Prime Minister of the United Kingdom Rishi Sunak, 74 living billionaires, and 17 astronauts.[49] In academia, its alumni include the presidents and provosts of Yale, Harvard and Princeton. | Rank | Institution | Endowment Value | State |

## Key Insights:

**Harvard University** has the largest university endowment in the world at $49.444 billion, making it the wealthiest educational institution globally.

**Yale University** has the second-largest endowment at $41.383 billion. Notably, Yale's endowment has a reputation as one of the best-performing investment portfolios in American higher education and was established in 1718 from an initial fund of £562 provided by Elihu Yale.

**Top 3 universities alone** (Harvard, Yale, and Stanford) control over $127 billion in endowment assets combined.

**Performance**: Many of these top-endowed universities have strong investment returns. For example, Yale's endowment earned a 40.2% investment return in fiscal 2021, bringing its value to $42.3 billion at that time.

The data comes from the National Association of College and University Business Officers (NACUBO) for Fiscal Year 2022, which is the most recent comprehensive data available on Wikipedia. These endowments are invested in various financial instruments and provide crucial funding for university operations, scholarships, research, and other institutional priorities.
